tier_reason: The mpope9/exor_bechmark README Benchee output (code at lib/exor_benchmark.exs) lists xor8 8 1M at 1.55 ms/645.20 ips and xor16 10M at 1.77 ms/565.42 ips, against Bloomex, Blex and erbloom rows that match the record. CPU, Elixir and OTP are stated, and the exor_filter c_src Makefile defaults to -O3, but the C compiler is never named. It is first-party, laptop-run and non-independent, so it stays at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Benchee, 10,000 lookups per iteration: xor8 8 1M 1.55 ms avg (645.20 ips) vs Bloomex 1M 8.87 ms, Blex 1M 13.17 ms, erbloom 1M 4.01 ms (5.7x / 8.5x / 2.6x, derived from page data). xor16 10M 1.77 ms avg (565.42 ips) vs Bloomex 10M 15.24 ms, Blex 10M 18.47 ms, erbloom 10M 3.90 ms (8.6x / 10.4x / 2.2x, derived from page data). The page's own 'Comparison' column is relative to the fastest row (fuse8 100), not to exor_filter.
corrections.workload: mpope9/exor_bechmark Benchee shootout (lib/exor_benchmark.exs; exor_filter pinned to v0.5.2): filters of 100/1k/100k/1M/10M elements, 10,000 lookups per iteration, 2 s warmup and 5 s time, comparing exor_filter xor8/xor16 (and efuse_filter fuse8) against Bloomex, Blex and erbloom.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Elixir 1.12.2, Erlang/OTP 24.0.5. exor_filter is a C NIF (c_src/xor_filter_nif.c wrapping FastFilter xor_singleheader), not Rust; its c_src Makefile defaults to CFLAGS ?= -O3 -std=c99 -finline-functions. The C compiler and version are not stated. erbloom is a Rust NIF.
corrections.caveats: This is a non-independent benchmark by the library author, run on a laptop (the README warns about this). The Bloom baselines are not set to xor8's FPR: Bloomex scalable and erbloom are configured at 0.1 error and Blex at 0.01, while xor8 is about 0.39%. The page's ratio column is against the fastest row (fuse8), so the ratios versus Bloom are derived. xor8/xor16 belong to the xor-filter family; the qualifying comparison is against the Bloom libraries. The C compiler is not stated.

notes: The numbers match exactly. The fixes are: the ratios are now marked as derived, the NIF is C (the record said Rust), the size list includes 100, and the mismatched Bloom FPR settings are added to caveats. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, last commit 2021-12-02 (abandoned), 35 stars, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party measured numbers (about 7.6 bits/key; measured FPR 0.783% at r=7; construction 26.0 vs 60.4 ns/key at 10M on an i9-14900HX, benches/construct.rs). Its comparison against Bloom is only a qualitative memory statement, with no Bloom filter measured, so it is C. The companion paper repo integrallis/ribbon-catches-bloom is an unreviewed preprint in the NeurIPS template and does not change this.

corrections.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml and README; LICENSE plus LICENSE-APACHE present; GitHub detector reports MIT)
corrections.caveats: The Bloom comparison is qualitative: the README says ~7.6 bits/key at ~0.8% FPR is 'well under a Bloom filter's memory', and the companion paper (github.com/integrallis/ribbon-catches-bloom, unreviewed preprint) says 'a quarter less memory' based on theory rather than a measured Bloom filter. The ribbon filter is not faster than Bloom at construction. The paper measures pleated homogeneous ribbon at about 24 ns/key versus 6.1-11.5 ns/key for single-thread blocked-Bloom insertion at 100M keys, and it needs 16 threads to match a single Bloom thread. The only numeric head-to-head is pleated vs the crate's own arrival-order build (2.3x at 10M keys). Query speed against Bloom is not measured. The rustc version and flags are not stated (rust-version 1.87 is the MSRV). Very new project (1 star).

notes: The record is accurate. The benchmark_url anchor pointed to the construction section, which has no Bloom claim; the memory claim is in the README intro, so the URL now points to the README root. The companion paper repo may be worth tracking as a separate RocksDB-construction entry (1.78x faster Standard128 ribbon build than stock RocksDB), but that is a different baseline.

tier_reason: The README Benchmark tables match the record exactly (17,458.015 vs 8,879.024 q/ms for Long keys; 7,121.787 vs 5,318.409 for String keys; 123,042 vs 144,390 bytes). The JMH code (src/jmh/java/me/k11i/xorfilter/QueryBenchmark.java) confirms the baseline is Guava BloomFilter.create at fpp 0.00389 and 0.00002. No JVM, CPU or JMH settings are stated, so it is first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Long keys: 17,458.015 q/ms (xor8) vs 8,879.024 q/ms (Guava Bloom, fpp=0.389%), ~1.97x (derived from page data). String keys: 7,121.787 vs 5,318.409 q/ms, ~1.34x (derived from page data). Serialization: 123,042 bytes / 9.843 bits per entry (xor8) vs 144,390 bytes / 11.551 bits per entry (Bloom, fpp=0.389%), ~1.17x smaller (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: JMH (me.champeau.gradle.jmh 0.5.0, default settings, results in ms) query throughput over a 16,384-element filter (NUM_ELEMENTS = 1 << 14) for Long and String keys, plus serialization size (FppAndSerializationSize.java). Xor Filter (8-bit, 16-bit, Murmur128 via Guava Funnels) is compared against Guava 28.2-jre BloomFilter at fpp=0.389% and fpp=0.002%.
corrections.caveats: No JVM version, CPU model or JMH warmup/iteration/fork counts are documented; the build uses the plugin defaults. The ~1.97x/~1.34x throughput and ~1.17x size ratios are derived from page data. At equal target FPR the xor8 vs Bloom (0.389%) size gain is modest (9.843 vs 11.551 bits/entry). The Bintray repository in the README is defunct. The project has been unmaintained since 2020.

notes: The numbers and baseline are verified. Metadata confirmed: MIT, last commit 2020-01-23 (abandoned), 20 stars, not archived, not a fork. The corrections only make the workload more precise and mark the ratios as derived.
